{
  "headline": "UK MPs Deny Vote Against Animal Sentience Amendment Undermines Recognition of Animal Welfare",
  "date": "2023-11-20",
  "source": "The Guardian",
  "story": "Last week, MPs in the UK House of Commons voted against an amendment aimed at transferring the European Union's protocol on animal sentience into domestic law. The amendment was narrowly defeated by 313 votes to 295 on 15 November, sparking significant confusion and controversy over its implications for animal welfare recognition in the UK. Tory MP Zac Goldsmith described some of the media coverage surrounding the vote as \"weird and dishonest,\" clarifying on Twitter that the vote was about legal procedures to ensure ongoing animal welfare standards rather than a denial of animal sentience. Fellow Conservative MP Rachel Maclean also sought to dispel confusion, posting a video asserting that protecting animals as sentient beings is already entrenched in UK law and dismissing criticisms as \"fake news.\"\n\nPrime Minister Theresa May emphasized at the Wednesday Prime Minister's Questions session that the government fully recognizes and respects animals as sentient beings that must be treated accordingly. Environment Secretary Michael Gove reiterated this position in a letter shared by Tory MP Hugo Swire on social media, underscoring that no MP doubts that animals possess feelings or emotions.\n\nDespite these reassurances, the vote has galvanized protests from animal rights activists and numerous online petitions targeting the House of Lords, Parliament, and the Environment Secretary. Public figures such as presenter Sue Perkins have joined in criticizing the MPs' decision, highlighting the public concern about the issue. Gudrun Ravetz, senior vice-president of the British Veterinary Association, voiced alarm at the marginal majority against the amendment, warning it could undermine the UK's reputation for high standards in animal health and welfare post-Brexit.\n\nOn the other hand, Conservative MP Henry Smith defended the government’s stance by noting that existing EU laws permitted various practices opposed by animal rights groups. The defeated amendment, led by Green Party co-leader Caroline Lucas, sought to incorporate article 13 of title II of the Lisbon Treaty directly into UK legislation. During the parliamentary debate, Lucas emphasized that the recognition of animal sentience has been a long-standing part of EU law since the UK’s presidency of the EU in 1997, formally acknowledged in 1999.\n\nThe controversy highlights ongoing tensions about how animal welfare standards will be maintained after Brexit and the legal routes the UK government will use to uphold protections for animals recognized as sentient beings."
}
```
